passage: The rain started just as Rashmi's birthday party began, so thirty children were squeezed into one flat instead of the terrace. Nitin stood by the shoe rack for a long while, watching the games before he joined, and when he did, it was only the card game in the corner with Rashmi, his cousin and favourite person. He laughed hard at her cheating. By eight his head buzzed with the noise. On the auto ride home through the downpour he didn't speak. His mother asked, "Didn't you enjoy it?" "I did," he said. "I'm just full." At home he lay on his bed with the lamp on and a comic, and after half an hour he came out humming.

qa.q: Where did Nitin stand before joining the games?
qa.a: He stood by the shoe rack.

qa.q: What did Nitin mean when he said he was "just full"?
qa.a: He had enjoyed the party but felt drained by the noise and needed quiet, not comfort for sadness.

qa.q: What helped Nitin recover after the party, and why was it the right choice?
qa.a: Time alone on his bed with a comic restored him, and after half an hour he came out humming.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mother have read his silence in the auto?
qa.a: She seems to have worried he was unhappy, until he explained he had enjoyed it and was only worn out.

grounding: A boy watches a crowded party before joining one close cousin, then needs time alone to recover, not because he is unhappy.

passage: On the first day of the colony's summer drama camp, Yash sat on the clubhouse steps for twenty minutes, watching. He noticed who shouted, who helped, who got left out. By the second hour he had joined, but only the group with his old friend Nitin, making the paper crown for the king. The director called him "our shy one" in front of everyone, and he flushed. He wasn't sad; he was working out the room. By evening, after rehearsals and a loud snack break, he walked home slowly and went straight to the balcony with his sketchbook. Amma left him there. At dinner he talked for twenty minutes about the play.

qa.q: How long did Yash sit on the clubhouse steps?
qa.a: He sat on the clubhouse steps for twenty minutes, watching.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the director called him "our shy one" in front of everyone?
qa.a: He flushed, so he likely felt embarrassed at a label when he was really just working out the room.

qa.q: What choice did Amma make when Yash went to the balcony, and why did it help?
qa.a: She left him there with his sketchbook, giving him quiet to recover, and he came to dinner full of talk.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Yash's way of joining the camp?
qa.a: Nitin may see it as normal for an old friend who joins slowly but is happy once he has picked his people.

grounding: A boy watches a new group before joining one close friend, feels drained after a busy day and recovers alone, happily.

passage: On the first morning of summer camp at the community centre, the other children rushed to the craft tables. Dilnaz stood by the water cooler for twenty minutes, watching: who shared the glue, who grabbed, who laughed kindly. Aunty Rosy, the camp leader, came over, frowning. 'Aren't you happy here?' 'I am,' Dilnaz said. 'I'm just looking first.' Then she walked to the end of the table where one boy, Darshan, was carefully cutting paper birds, and sat beside him. By Friday they were a pair, finishing each other's kites, and she still spent snack break reading alone on the steps, humming.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz stand on the first morning?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz watch for twenty minutes before joining?
qa.a: She felt calmer seeing the group first and noticing who was kind; she wasn't unhappy, just careful.

qa.q: How could Aunty Rosy support a child like Dilnaz?
qa.a: Trust her 'I'm just looking first', give her time, and not treat reading alone at snack break as a problem.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Dilnaz sitting down beside him?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt glad to have one steady friend who shared his careful way of working.

grounding: Shows a child who watches a new group before joining, prefers one close friend, and enjoys time alone without being unhappy.

passage:
Saturday night. At his cousin's sangeet, Ojas danced, laughed with the cousins and ate three helpings of jalebi. By eleven his ears rang and his smile felt stuck on.
Sunday. He stayed in his room all morning with a comic and the door half shut. 'Are you sad, Ojas?' Mummy asked, peering in. 'No. Just empty. Not a bad empty. I need quiet.' She left a glass of lassi and closed the door.
Monday. After school he cycled to Amandeep's, his one best friend. They built a ramp for two hours, barely talking, and Ojas came home humming.

qa.q: What did Ojas eat three helpings of at the sangeet?
qa.a: Jalebi.

qa.q: How was Ojas feeling on Sunday morning, in his own words?
qa.a: He felt drained, 'empty' but not sad; he needed quiet to recover after the busy party.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Ojas recover?
qa.a: She asked instead of assuming, then left lassi and closed the door, giving him the solitude he needed.

qa.q: What might Amandeep enjoy about Monday's ramp-building with Ojas?
qa.a: Amandeep seems comfortable with long, easy silences, so two hours of building side by side felt good for both.

grounding: Shows a child who enjoys a busy party but is drained afterwards, recovers through solitude, and prefers one close friend.

passage: Jeevan, you ask why I slipped away from the Diwali party last night. Your Sonali Aaji was the same at ten, in our chawl in Pune. At every festival there were fifty people in two rooms, and I loved them all, for about an hour. Then my head would fill up like a pot boiling over, and I would slip away to the stairwell with a book. My mother called it rudeness. 'Why are you so unfriendly? People will talk.' I wasn't unhappy. I was full. One Diwali my Mavshi found me on the stairs and read beside me without a word. After a while I went back in, laughing again. She told my mother, 'Let her have the stairs. She comes back better.' From then on, the stairs were mine.

qa.q: Where did Sonali go when her head filled up?
qa.a: To the stairwell with a book.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when her mother called her unfriendly?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and misunderstood, because she wasn't unhappy, only full.

qa.q: What turning point made the stairs Sonali's?
qa.a: Her Mavshi sat and read with her, saw her come back laughing, and told her mother to let her have the stairs.

qa.q: How might Sonali's mother have felt at those festivals?
qa.a: Her mother seems worried about what people would say, reading Sonali's slipping away as rudeness.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a child who enjoys people but is drained by busy gatherings and recovers through solitude, not unhappiness.

passage: At her cousin's wedding, the generator failed during the sangeet and the hall went dark and even noisier. Vidya, nine, stood by the wall and watched while the other children screamed and ran around with phone torches. She didn't join at first. She noticed who was bossy, who was kind. Then her cousin Chinmay, her one close friend in the family, came to stand beside her. "Want to hold the torch together?" They made shadow animals on the wall for an hour, laughing. By ten she was worn out. While the dancing went on, she slipped up to the terrace with a shawl and sat alone under the stars. When her mother came up, worried, Vidya smiled. "I'm happy, Ma. I just need quiet now."

qa.q: What did Vidya and Chinmay make on the wall?
qa.a: Shadow animals.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel by ten o'clock?
qa.a: She felt tired and drained after the busy evening, though still happy.

qa.q: Why was going to the terrace a good choice for Vidya?
qa.a: Quiet time alone helped her recover her energy after a noisy, crowded party.

qa.q: How might Vidya's mother have felt finding her on the terrace?
qa.a: She may have been worried at first, then reassured when Vidya said she was happy and just needed quiet.

grounding: Shows a quiet child who watches a new group before joining, prefers one close friend and recovers from a busy party through solitude, not unhappiness, despite a power failure.
